props.title: All the Fine Young Cannibals

sections.content: **All the Fine Young Cannibals (1960)** (1960) represents a fascinating intersection of youth rebellion cinema and Southern melodrama, starring Robert Wagner and Natalie Wood at the height of their fame. The film's misleading title - it has nothing to do with actual cannibalism - echoes the era's tendency to use provocative marketing to draw audiences. Like Peyton Place (1957) and A Summer Place (1959), it explores forbidden love and generational conflict in the conservative 1950s American South, though with notably less success than those contemporaries.

sections.content: The film's treatment of jazz music and religious conflict feels particularly dated now but offers insight into how Hollywood depicted Southern culture during this period. Director Michael Anderson, fresh off the success of **Around the World in 80 Days** (1956), struggled to bring coherence to the scattered narrative. However, the chemistry between real-life couple Wagner and Wood occasionally elevates the material, presaging their later reunion in **The Great Race** (1965).

What's most interesting about **All the Fine Young Cannibals** (1960) is how it fits into the broader pattern of "youth in rebellion" films that dominated the late 1950s and early 1960s. While not as explosive as **Rebel Without a Cause** (1955) or as provocative as **Wild in the Streets** (1968), it attempts to bridge the gap between traditional melodrama and the emerging youth culture cinema that would soon revolutionize Hollywood. SUBHEAD: The Natalie Wood Factor

The film represents an important moment in Natalie Wood's evolution from child star to serious adult actress. Coming between her breakthrough in **Rebel Without a Cause** (1955) and her triumph in **West Side Story** (1961), **All the Fine Young Cannibals** (1960) shows Wood pushing against her ingenue image. Her portrayal of Chad Bixby's love interest demonstrates the emotional depth that would later serve her well in films like **Love with the Proper Stranger** (1963) and **Inside Daisy Clover** (1965).
